faq.q: What is the normal TSB range in a term newborn after 24 h?

faq.a: When TSB exceeds the Bhutani nomogram thresholds for age and weight.
faq.q: When is phototherapy indicated in a term infant?

faq.a: It identifies immune haemolysis, guiding treatment and monitoring.
faq.q: Why is a direct Coombs test important?

exam: A 3‑day‑old term infant has TSB 280 µmol/L and is feeding well. What is the next step? — Initiate phototherapy; monitor TSB every 6–12 h.
A 2‑day‑old infant has TSB 350 µmol/L and a rising trend of 12 µmol/L in 2 h. What is the urgent intervention? — Exchange transfusion.
Why is a direct Coombs test performed in a jaundiced newborn? — To detect alloimmune haemolysis; a positive result changes management.
A newborn has conjugated bilirubin 30% of TSB. What is the most likely diagnosis? — Neonatal hepatitis or biliary atresia; further imaging needed.
Which drug should be avoided in a neonate with hyperbilirubinaemia? — Paracetamol in high doses, as it can worsen hepatic injury.
A 4‑month‑old child presents with jaundice and a history of malaria treatment. What is the most likely cause? — Hemolysis from antimalarial drugs or malaria‑induced hemolysis.
ai.title: Total Serum Bilirubin in Paediatrics
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Total serum bilirubin measures the overall bilirubin load in a child’s blood. It helps distinguish physiologic jaundice from pathologic causes, guides phototherapy, and flags severe hyperbilirubinaemia that may lead to kernicterus.

b: TSB < 20 µmol/L (0.3 mg/dL) is normal in a newborn after 24 h
sections.p: Total serum bilirubin (TSB) is the sum of unconjugated and conjugated bilirubin in plasma. It is measured by a diazo or enzymatic assay and expressed in µmol/L or mg/dL.

t.b: >15% of TSB or >2 mg/dL indicates conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia

sections.p: The Bhutani nomogram guides phototherapy thresholds in term infants. In low‑resource settings, a simplified 2‑hour rise of >10 µmol/L or a TSB >200 µmol/L warrants urgent review.

b: Congenital liver disease – biliary atresia, neonatal hepatitis
sections.p: In East Africa, the top causes of hyperbilirubinaemia are haemolysis, infection, and liver immaturity. Consider local endemic diseases and herbal remedies.
Jaundice appears as yellow discoloration of sclera, skin, and mucosa. In severe cases, the infant may be lethargic, have poor feeding, or display seizures.
Use the table to decide which test answers which clinical question. If a test is unavailable, use clinical judgment and basic labs.

t.b: Positive direct Coombs indicates alloimmune hemolysis
Elevated transaminases suggest hepatitis or drug toxicity
Dilated ducts or gallbladder wall thickening

sections.p: Rapid rise, conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, or neurological signs require immediate action. Kernicterus is irreversible and fatal if untreated.

b: Avoid hepatotoxic drugs – e.g., paracetamol overdose
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first. Supportive care includes phototherapy, hydration, and monitoring. Avoid drugs that increase bilirubin or cause hepatotoxicity.
Re‑check TSB after 6–24 h if risk factors are present. Educate caregivers on feeding, sun exposure, and avoiding herbal remedies.

b: Hemolytic disease – unconjugated, with anemia and reticulocytosis
sections.p: Physiologic jaundice, neonatal hepatitis, and hemolytic disease of the newborn can mimic each other. Use direct bilirubin and Coombs to differentiate.

b: Confirm with repeat test if results are unexpected
sections.p: Low albumin can falsely lower TSB. Hemolysis during sampling can raise unconjugated bilirubin. Inadequate calibration of photometers can misread TSB.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe hyperbilirubinaemia (TSB >300 µmol/L), rapid rise, conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, seizures, lethargy, poor feeding
